research_study_list.title: Q-DM: An Efficient Low-bit Quantized Diffusion Model
Towards Accurate Post-training Quantization for Diffusion Models
research_study_list.abstract:
In this paper, we propose an accurate data-free post-training quantization
framework of diffusion models (ADP-DM) for efficient image generation.
Conventional data-free quantization methods learn shared quantization functions
for tensor discretization regardless of the generation timesteps, while the
activation distribution differs significantly across various timesteps. The
calibration images are acquired in random timesteps which fail to provide
sufficient information for generalizable quantization function learning. Both
issues cause sizable quantization errors with obvious image generation
performance degradation. On the contrary, we design group-wise quantization
functions for activation discretization in different timesteps and sample the
optimal timestep for informative calibration image generation, so that our
quantized diffusion model can reduce the discretization errors with negligible
computational overhead. Specifically, we partition the timesteps according to
the importance weights of quantization functions in different groups, which are
optimized by differentiable search algorithms. We also select the optimal
timestep for calibration image generation by structural risk minimizing
principle in order to enhance the generalization ability in the deployment of
quantized diffusion model. Extensive experimental results show that our method
outperforms the state-of-the-art post-training quantization of diffusion model
by a sizable margin with similar computational cost.
research_study_list.full_text: Towards Accurate Post-training Quantization for Diffusion Models Changyuan Wang1, Ziwei Wang 3, Xiuwei Xu 2, Yansong Tang1*, Jie Zhou 2, Jiwen Lu 2 1Shenzhen Key Laboratory of Ubiquitous Data Enabling, Shenzhen International Graduate School, Tsinghua University, China 2Department of Automation, Tsinghua University, China 3Carnegie Mellon University {wangchan22@mails.,xxw21@mails.,tang.yansong@sz.,jzhou@,lujiwen@}tsinghua.edu.cn; ziweiwa2@andrew.cmu.edu Abstract In this paper, we propose an accurate post-training quan- tization framework of diffusion models (APQ-DM) for effi- cient image generation. Conventional quantization frame- works learn shared quantization functions for tensor dis- cretization regardless of the generation timesteps in diffusion models, while the activation distribution differs significantly across various timesteps. Meanwhile, the calibration im- ages are acquired in random timesteps which fail to provide sufficient information for generalizable quantization func- tion learning. Both issues cause sizable quantization errors with obvious image generation performance degradation. On the contrary, we design distribution-aware quantization functions for activation discretization in different timesteps and search the optimal timesteps for informative calibra- tion image generation, so that our quantized diffusion model can reduce the discretization errors with negligible computa- tional overhead. Specifically, we partition various timestep quantization functions into different groups according to the importance weights, which are optimized by differentiable search algorithms. We also extend structural risk minimiza- tion principle for informative calibration image generation to enhance the generalization ability in the deployment of quantized diffusion model. Extensive experimental results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art post- training quantization of diffusion model by a sizable margin with similar computational cost1. 1. Introduction Denoising diffusion generative models [ 11, 32] have achieved outstanding performance in a wide variety of com- puter vision tasks such as image edition [2, 28], style transfor- mation [34, 38], image super-resolution [18, 30] and many *Corresponding author. 1Code is available at https://github.com/ChangyuanWang17/APQ-DM Figure 1. (a) Existing methods leverage shared quantization for activation discretization across different timesteps with significant quantization errors, while we divide timesteps into groups with specific rounding functions for each partition. (b) Conventional methods construct calibration set by randomly image selecting with ineffective supervision, while we actively sample timesteps based on the structural risk minimization (SRM) principle. others. Compared with the generative adversarial networks (GAN), diffusion models obtained recovered contents with better quality and diversity on most downstream tasks. How- ever, diffusion models usually require hundreds of noise arXiv:2305.18723v4  [cs.CV]  30 Apr 2024evaluation steps to generate high-quality images from Gaus- sian noises by neural networks with millions of parameters, and the numerous forward passes in network inference re- sult in heavy computation burden. Therefore, designing lightweight denoising process for diffusion models is highly demanded for flexible deployment in practical applications with limited resources such as mobile phones and robots. To accelerate the generation process of diffusion mod- els, recent studies made significant efforts in decreasing the sampling times of image denoising process [3, 14, 33] and reducing the network complexity in noise estimation of each step [19, 20, 31]. The former removes redundant steps in the reverse process of diffusion, and the latter extends the network compression techniques to noise estimation such as pruning [12, 40] and quantization [13, 17] for acceleration. We focus on the latter by quantizing the noise estimation networks with integer arithmetic inference. Due to the in- tractability of the training data and the unbearable training cost of diffusion models to fully optimize quantized net- work parameters, the post-training quantization framework for the pre-trained full-precision decoders is leveraged that only learns the rounding function parameters. Nevertheless, conventional data-free post-training quantization methods [5, 42] learn a shared layer-wise rounding function for all generation timesteps where the activation distribution varies obviously in diffusion models, and the calibration images are generated in random timesteps which fails to provide sufficient information to acquire generalizable quantization function. Consequently, both the inaccurate quantization functions and uninformative calibration images lead to signif- icant quantization errors in noise estimation process, which degrades the synthesis performance by a sizable margin. In this paper, we present an accurate post-training quanti- zation framework for diffusion models in order to achieve efficient image generation. Different from existing methods that leverage shared layer-wise quantization functions for all timesteps and synthesizing calibration images in random timesteps for training, we partition timesteps into different groups to impose specific rounding functions for each group and sampling the optimal timesteps to generate informative calibrate images for quantization parameter learning. There- fore, the significant quantization errors of noise estimation in diffusion model deployment can be reduced with only negli- gible computation overhead. More specifically, we employ a differentiable search strategy to acquire the optimal group assignment for different generation timesteps, and learns in- dividual rounding functions for each group with minimized discretization errors. For the differentiable search, the ac- tivations quantized by discretization functions in different groups are summed with learnable importance weights. We also generalize the structural risk minimization (SRM) princi- ple for timestep selection to generate informative calibration images, where the entropy of rounding function weights in differentiable search and the sampling times of the timestep are considered as the criteria based on our formulation. Fig- ure 1 demonstrates the comparison between our method and conventional data-free post-training quantization framework for diffusion models. Extensive experimental results on unconditioned synthesis and conditional image generation across various network architectures clearly demonstrate that our method sizably increases the quality of the generated images with only negligible computational complexity. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We propose an accurate and efficient post-training quan- tization framework for pre-trained diffusion models that preserve the generation performance in image generation with 6-bit weights and activations. • We present the distribution-aware quantization and activate timestep selection function to significantly reduce quanti- zation errors across generation timesteps and search the representative calibration images according to structural risk minimization principle, so that the rounding functions can be optimized with more informative supervision. • We conduct extensive experiments on a wide variety of datasets for image generation, and the results clearly demonstrate the superiority of the presented method. 2. Related Work Efficient diffusion models: Diffusion models achieve more satisfying quality and diversity in image generation com- pared with GANs, while the generation efficiency is signifi- cantly decreased due to the iterative noise evaluation process with long timesteps. The denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) [11] leverages a forward pass for noise per- turbation and a reverse process for image denoising. Existing methods mainly focus on leveraging a shorter sampling path without sizable performance degradation, which can be di- vided into two categories including convergence speedup and sampling path selection. Convergence speedup methods aim to discretize the stochastic differential equations (SDE) or the ordinary differential equations (ODE) with minimized discretization errors. Song et al. [32] modeled the diffusion model with a non-Markov process that considers the original images for noise perturbation, where the convergence for im- age generation speeds up sizably. Bao et al. [3] formulated an analytic form of variance and KL divergence based on a pre-trained score-based model that simultaneously enhanced the log-likelihood and the generation speed. Sampling path selection usually chooses partial timesteps in the denoising process regarding the learning objectives. Watson et al. [35] searched the best K sampling timesteps for noise evaluation via dynamic programming, where the goal was to maximize the evidence lower bound (ELBO) in the reverse process. Due to the inconsistent performance between the training ELBO and the generation quality, they further presented Kernel Inception Distance (KID) [ 36] as the optimizationCalibration Image Generation Selected TimeStep 𝒕𝒊 Distribution-aware Quantization  Pre-trained  Model Decoder Input  Feature Map Output  Feature MapGroup 1 Group 2 Group 3 𝜎1 𝑡1   Differentiable Search framework TimeStep Selection Importance Weight Entropy 3 1 ⋯ 35 1 Sampling Times 𝝉1 𝝉2 𝝉3 ⋯ 𝝉𝑇−1 𝝉𝑇 Selection Criteria Selected TimeStep 𝒕𝒊+𝟏 Feature  Distribution 0.2𝑇 0.8𝑇 𝜎2 𝑡1   𝜎3 𝑡1   𝜎1 𝑡2   𝜎2 𝑡2   𝜎3 𝑡2   ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ TimeStep 𝝉 Entropy ⋯ Figure 2. The overall pipeline of our method. The calibration images are generated according to the selected timesteps, and activations in the pre-trained diffusion models are parallelly quantized by rounding functions of all groups. The output feature maps are acquired by adding the quantized value with the importance weights, where the quantization parameters and the importance weights are jointly optimized. The importance weight entropy and the sampling times are considered in the timestep selection criteria to decide the optimal timestep for calibration image generation in the next round. objective to differentiably search the sampling timesteps. In this paper, we aim to reduce the complexity of single-step denoising process by quantization, which is orthogonal to the acceleration techniques of sampling path shortening. Network quantization: Network quantization has aroused extensive interest in computer vision due to the significant reduction in storage and computational cost, as the full-precision variables are substituted by quantized val- ues and the multiply-add (MAC) operations are replaced by integer arithmetics. Quantization-aware training (QAT) [6, 24] finetunes the quantized network with training dataset of full-precision models. Due to the inaccessibility of the full training set and the extremely high training cost, post- training quantization (PTQ) [10, 21, 25, 26] that optimizes the rounding functions with a small calibration set is more practical in realistic applications. Choukroun et al. [7] minimized the l2 distance between the quantized and full- precision tensors to avoid obvious task performance degra- dation, and Zhao et al. [41] duplicated the channels with outliers and halved the value so that the clipping loss could be reduced without increasing the rounding errors. Liu et al. [25] preserved the relative ranking orders of the self- attention in vision transformers to prevent information loss in post-training quantization, and explored mixed-precision quantization strategy according to the nuclear norm of atten- tion map and features. Zero-shot PTQ further extends the limits that efficiently quantize neural networks without any real image data. Cai et al. [5] optimized the pixel values of the generated images to enforce the statistics of sample batches to mimic the batch normalization (BN) layers in the full-precision networks. Li et al. [22] further extended PTQ framework to transformer architectures by diversifying the self-attention of different patches with patch similarity metrics. As Shang et al. [31] and Li et al. [20] observed, different activation distribution across timesteps and the ef- fectiveness change of calibration images acquired in various timesteps amplify the quantization errors in existing methods. To avoid the overfitting of the step-wise quantization caused by limited calibration samples, we present the distribution- aware quantization for diffusion models across timesteps with significantly reduced learnable parameters. Meanwhile, different from [31] that manually assigned the timestep index for calibration generation, we generalize the structural risk minimization principle to discover the optimal timesteps. 3. Approach In this section, we first introduce the preliminaries of post- training quantization for diffusion models and then detail the distribution-aware quantization across generation timesteps with the differentiable search framework. Finally, we demon- strate the timestep selection for calibration image generation according to the structural risk minimization principle. 3.1. Network Quantization Diffusion models leverage a forward pass to impose noise on images and a reverse pass to transform Gaussian noise into an image for generation. Denoting the real data as x0 and the latent image at the tth step as xt, the probability of the forward process can be represented as follows: q(xt|xt−1) = N(xt| p 1 − βtxt−1, βtI), (1) where βt means the variance schedule at the tth step that indicates imposed Gaussian noise to the latent image. When the total number of forward steps denoted as T becomes large enough, the latent image xT can be regarded as the standard Gaussian noise. We leverage an approximated con- dition distribution pθ(xt−1|xt) to generate the latent imagein reverse process due to the intractability of true distribution q(xt−1|xt), where the approximated distribution is parame- terized by neural networks with weight θ: pθ(xt−1|xt) = N(xt−1|µθ,t(xt), Σθ,t(xt)). (2) The training process of diffusion model aims to minimize the negative log-likelihood with the evidence lower bound optimization in variational inference: LV LB= Eq(x0:T )[log q(x1:T |x0) pθ(x0:T ) ] ⩾ −Eq(x0) log pθ(x0). (3) In the practical applications, iterative noise estimation pro- cess is implemented with the diffusion model for content generation, and the heavy computational cost of the reverse phase disables the deployment in resource-constrained de- vices such as mobile phones and robots. To accelerate the denoising process for each reverse step, post-training quanti- zation leverages a small calibration set to learn the rounding function parameters for weights and activations of the de- coder, where the quantization function can be represented as follows: ˆx = s · Φ([x/s] , zmin, zmax), (4) where x and ˆx represent real-valued and quantized matrix respectively. [·] means the rounding function to the nearest integer and Φ is the clipping operation that regularizes the element into the range from zmin to zmax. The quantization scaling parameter s indicates the interval between adjacent rounding points. As empirically demonstrated in [ 31], the activation distribution varies significantly across different timesteps during the reverse process, and the shared rounding functions usually cause severe quantization errors for image generation. Moreover, randomly selecting the timestep to generate latent images for calibration set construction fails to provide sufficient information for generalizable quantization function learning. 3.2. Distribution-aware Quantization for Diverse Activation Distribution Since the activation distribution changes significantly across timesteps, discretizing the full-precision intermediate fea- tures in similar data distribution with the same quantization functions can reduce the quantization errors. We first de- scribe the distribution-aware quantization scheme and then illustrate the differentiable group assignment of timesteps. Shared quantization functions may cause large clipping errors for widely distributed activations and rounding errors for narrowly distributed ones. Directly assigning specific rounding functions for network activations in each timestep leads to overfitting in optimization because of the limited cal- ibration samples, and quantizing activations in the timestep where optimal quantization range is similar with the same rounding functions can achieve better trade-off between the quantization accuracy and rounding function generalizability. Assuming partitioning all T timesteps into C groups, the quantization strategy can be written in the following: ˆx = sg(i) · Φ(  x/sg(i)  , zg(i) min, zg(i) max), (5) where g(i) represents the assigned group for activations in the ith timestep. Meanwhile, sg(i), zg(i) min and zg(i) max respec- tively stand for scale parameters, the lower bound and the up- per bound of quantization for activations in the ith timestep. Assigning the optimal group indexes for different timesteps is critical in distribution-aware quantization to reduce the quantization errors without obvious computation overhead. Since enumerating assignment permutation is NP-hard to find the optimal solution, we extend the differentiable search framework to efficiently partition timesteps with minimal quantization errors. In the differentiable search, the latent images are quantized by all quantization functions, whose output values are summed with learnable importance weights to form the input for the next layer in the diffusion model: ˆx = GX g=1 σgsg · Φ([x/sg] , zg min, zg max), (6) where σg means the importance weight of the quantiza- tion function for the cth group with the normalizationPG g=1 σg = 1. When the training process completes, the rounding function with the largest importance weight is se- lected to be the search results for group-wise quantization. Despite the noise estimation loss of diffusion models, we also enforce the importance weights to approach zero or one by minimizing the entropy to avoid discretization er- rors in rounding function selection. The overall optimiza- tion objective J is written as follows, where we denote ϵθ(√αtx0 + √1 − αtϵ, t) as ϵθ for simplicity: min t,x0,ϵ J = Jd + λJe = ||ϵ − ϵθ||2 2 + λ GX g=1 −σt g log σt g, (7) where Jd and Je respectively represent the simplified variational lower bound of diffusion model objective and the discretization minimization loss in differentiable search, and the hyperparameter λ balances the importance of different terms. σt g demonstrates the importance weights of the quan- tization function for the gth group in the tth timestep. The noise ϵ from standard Gaussian distribution is approximated by the predicted noise ϵθ in the optimization objective. The diffusion parameter αt = Qt i−1 1 − βi controls the strength of noise in diffusion. We jointly update the parameters in quantization functions and the importance weights until con- vergence or achieving the maximal iteration steps, and the discretized hypernetwork is directly employed to generate images efficiently.3.3. TimeStep Selection for Calibration Generation The pipeline of post-training quantization for iterative re- verse process in diffusion models differs significantly from that in conventional vision models. Leveraging latent im- ages in all timesteps leads to unbearable training cost for quantization function learning, and latent images in adjacent timesteps can only offer redundant information for param- eter optimization. On the contrary, randomly select part of the timesteps usually fails to provide sufficient supervision that is representative to demonstrate the real distribution of the latent images. Therefore, it is desirable to actively sam- ple the timesteps to generate latent images for quantization parameter learning with effective guidance. We generate rep- resentative samples by structural risk minimization, which minimize the distance between selected and real distribution. We first introduce the extension of SRM principle to active timestep selection, and then formulate the selection criteria that can be feasibly computed. Structural risk minimization principle minimizes the up- per bound of the true risk on unseen data distribution, where the bound can be written as follows for a dataset containing n samples with the probability at least 1 − δ[4]: E(J(x)) ⩽ E(J(x)) + 2Rn(F) + r ln 1/δ n , (8) where E(J(x)) and E(J(x)) respectively illustrate the true expectation of the risk J for real data distribution x and the empirical expectation of that for sampled data from x, and Rn(F) is the Rademacher complexity over the function class F. The SRM principle requires the data to be sampled from i.i.d. distribution, while the latent images in selected timesteps should be more informative and representative. Therefore, we rewrite the SRM principle in the following way, where the detailed formulation is in the supplementary: E(J) ⩽ ES(J) + MMD (p(X), p(Xs)) + R0, (9) where we omit the data distribution x for simplicity. ES(J) denotes the empirical risk of the latent images of selected timesteps for noise estimation, and R0 demonstrates the complexity of the diffusion model in the reverse process. X and Xs stand for the distribution of latent images generated in all timesteps and the selected ones. The maximal mean discrepancy between two distributions p(X) and p(Xs) is represented as MMD (p(X), p(Xs)), which demonstrates the generalization ability of the calibration sets for quan- tization learning. The first criteria acquired by worst-case empirical risk of sampled latent images is formulated as follows for timesteps selection : min t,xt ES(J) = X xt∈S Jd + λJe, (10) where S represents the images selected in the calibration set, and J is the optimization objective defined in (7). This for- mula aims to train the highly quantified diffusion model with the constructed calibration sets. Since the original latent xT can be regarded as the standard Gaussian noise without bias, the objective Jd does not affect the worst-case empirical risk with different timesteps. The variance of Je influences the worst-case empirical risk across timesteps, because the en- tropy of the importance weights of distribution-aware quan- tization functions changes with the timesteps. Therefore, the criteria s1 from the empirical risk minimization can be trans- formed to selecting the timestep with the highest entropy of importance weights as s1 = PG g=1 −σt g log σt g. Meanwhile, The definition of maximal mean dis- crepancy can be written as follows, where we denote MMD (p(X), p(Xs)) as M for simplicity: min t M = sup || 1 |U| X xt∈U ϵθ − 1 |S| X xt∈S ϵθ|| = φ Nt + 1 ∝ 1 Nt + 1, (11) where U means the full set containing all original latent and timesteps for calibrating image selection, and | · |represents the number of elements in the set. φ is a constant in timestep sampling and Nt denotes the number of sampling times for the tth timestep in calibration set construction. Because the estimated noise of the samples in the full set is intractable, we utilize the number of sampling times to optimize the max- imal mean discrepancy based on upper confidence bound (UCB) principle [1] which achieves exploitation-exploration trade-off when sampling. A detailed derivation of the for- mula (11) can be found in the supplementary material. For the timestep when we sample a large number of latent images for calibration set construction, the maximal mean discrep- ancy becomes low as we acquire sufficient information of the latent image distribution in this timestep. Therefore, we ex- plore latent images in the timestep with few sampling times to further minimize the maximal mean discrepancy with high marginal benefits. The criteria s2 from the maximal mean discrepancy is designed as s2 = 1/(Nt + 1). The overall timestep selection criteria can be written as follows: max t s = s1 + ηs2 = GX g=1 −σt g log σt g + η Nt + 1, (12) where η is a hyperparameter to balance the importance of empirical risk and maximal mean discrepancy. The overall pipeline of our method is depicted in Figure 2. With the op- timally selected timesteps, the generated calibration images can provide effective supervision for quantization function learning, which can be well generalized in deployment. 4. LSQ learns the optimal quantization step sizes with minimized discretization errors, while the shared quantization policy across timesteps and randomly constructed calibration set in diffusion models leads to sig- nificant quantization loss. PTQ4DM and Q-diffusion employ the step-wise quantization functions to minimize the quanti- zation errors of the diversely distributed activations across timesteps, and presents heuristic timesteps selection criteria for calibration image generation. However, the optimization of large-scale learnable parameters faces the challenges of overfitting due to the very limited quantity of calibration sam- ples, and the data-independent calibration set construction cannot guarantee the optimality of the calibration images. As a result, our method outperforms PTQ4DM by 0.32 (2.55 vs. 2.23) and 1.02 (6.46 vs. 7.48) for IS and FID in LSUN- Bedroom respectively. Conclusion In this paper, we have presented a novel post-training quan- tization framework of diffusion model for efficient image generation. We design a differentiable search framework that assigns the optimal partition for each timestep, where network activations are discretized with distribution-aware quantization functions for rounding error minimization. By generalizing the structural risk minimization principle, we se- lect the optimal timesteps for calibration image construction to provide effective supervision in quantization parameter learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our meth- ods outperform the state-of-the-art post-training quantization methods across various diffusion architectures. llm_extracted_info.main_contributions: The paper proposes APQ-DM, an accurate post-training quantization framework for diffusion models, addressing significant quantization errors caused by varying activation distributions across generation timesteps and uninformative calibration images in conventional methods. APQ-DM introduces distribution-aware quantization functions for different timestep groups and actively searches for optimal timesteps to generate informative calibration images based on the structural risk minimization principle. This approach reduces discretization errors, preserves image generation quality with negligible computational overhead, and achieves high performance even at low bitwidths (e.g., 6-bit weights and activations).
llm_extracted_info.methodology: The APQ-DM framework comprises distribution-aware quantization and active timestep selection. Distribution-aware quantization partitions generation timesteps into groups, each assigned specific rounding functions optimized for their distinct activation distributions. A differentiable search framework with learnable importance weights and an entropy-based discretization minimization loss is used for optimal group assignment and quantization parameter learning. Active timestep selection generalizes the Structural Risk Minimization (SRM) principle to guide the generation of informative calibration images. The selection criteria combine minimizing empirical risk (by selecting timesteps with high importance weight entropy) and minimizing the maximal mean discrepancy between actual and sampled latent image distributions (by prioritizing timesteps with fewer sampling times).
llm_extracted_info.experimental_setup: Experiments were conducted on pre-trained DDIM and LDM diffusion models, configured for 100 iterative denoising timesteps. Quantization was applied uniformly at 6-bit and 8-bit for both weights and activations, with timesteps partitioned into eight groups. Calibration sets of 1024 images were used, with hyperparameters λ=0.8 and η=1.5. Performance was evaluated on unconditional image generation using Cifar-10, CelebA, LSUN-Church Outdoor, and LSUN-Bedroom datasets, and on class-conditional ImageNet generation. Evaluation metrics included Inception Score (IS), FID score, and sFID. The method's effectiveness was compared against state-of-the-art post-training quantization techniques such as LSQ, PTQ4DM, and Q-Diffusion, complemented by ablation studies on the number of groups, timestep sampling strategies, and hyperparameter sensitivity.
llm_extracted_info.limitations: The framework operates under the inherent limitations of post-training quantization, such as the intractability of full training data and the high cost associated with quantization-aware training for diffusion models. While the method addresses overfitting concerns by grouping timesteps, it still relies on a relatively small calibration set. A notable limitation is the introduction of hyperparameters (λ and η) whose optimal tuning is critical for performance, with the model demonstrating particular sensitivity to λ. Furthermore, the theoretical derivation for timestep selection involves practical simplifications which might affect its strict adherence to the structural risk minimization principle.

Open Problems: O-1  The permanent early-stop of SYMPHONY’s Recurrent Convergence Predictor (RCP) is irrevocable; a single false-positive skip irreversibly corrupts later denoising but the framework offers no rollback or certified error bound.
O-2  RCP’s TTL loss is heuristic.  A formal connection between the predicted residual norm, the Lipschitz constant of the denoiser, and the final x₀ error is missing, preventing skip decisions with statistical guarantees.
O-3  Basis selection is image-global.  Real-world pictures mix textures (e.g. hair) and flats (sky); an adaptive transform should vary per *patch* and *time-step* yet remain NPU-friendly.
O-4  μLC compresses user LoRA but leaves the  UNet untouched; >200 MB of frozen weights must still be fetched, blocking deployment on sub-8 GB devices.
O-5  Life-cycle carbon is tracked, yet *network* externalities (prompt upload, cloud fallback) and user-side rebound effects are ignored—carbon accounting is still incomplete.
O-6  The vestibular metric covers flicker but not rolling-shutter artefacts that occur when renders are streamed progressively; low-vision users report discomfort.

Methods: We propose CADENCE – Certifiably-Adaptive Diffusion with Error-bounds, Neural-compression & Carbon-Equity – a successor to SYMPHONY that tackles the above gaps.
A  Dual-Threshold Certifiable Skipper (DTCS)
   • For every patch-band we compute an *upper* bound ϵ̂ₜ on the L₂ error of the current latent using local Lipschitz estimates (spectral norm of Jacobian via power iteration) and predicted residual rₜ.  Execution is skipped only if rₜ<τ₁ *and* ϵ̂ₜ<τ₂, guaranteeing ‖x̂₀−x₀‖₂≤ϵ̂ₜ with ≥99 % confidence; otherwise the block is revisited one step later, enabling automatic rollback.
B  ReDo – Reversible Decoder Overlay
   • Replace the last two UNet scales with invertible 1×1 coupling layers so that skipped computations can be reconstructed backward on demand without re-running the encoder, enabling lossless rollback at <3 % MAC overhead.
C  Hierarchical Basis Mixer (HBM)
   • A light MoE selects {Haar, 8×8 DCT, learned Givens} per *4×4 patch* and *denoising stage* using a shared key–value router executed in INT4.  Gates are regularised by a FLOP penalty to stay NPU-friendly; kernels are pre-tiled so switching costs one tensor pointer swap.
D  TinyUNet-KD
   • Distil the frozen 860 M-param teacher into a 96 M param INT4 student using multi-step moment matching and feature imitation, then apply μLC on top. Total on-device footprint <60 MB incl. 20 personal styles, enabling RAM-strapped handsets.
E  Carbon Ripple Tracker (CRT)
   • Extends xLCM with two new terms: (i) network energy E_net estimated from real-time uplink kB × carrier-specific J/MB, (ii) *rebound* factor R that models extra user sessions unlocked by faster sampling (learnt via causal bandit from usage logs).  CRT reports *marginal* gCO₂/image, allowing policy interventions.
F  Rolling-Comfort Index (RCI)
   • Simulates progressive scan-out and models retinal integration to predict discomfort from line-wise luminance jumps.  Scheduler keeps RCI<0.4 while optimising FPS.
G  Meta-Device Learner (MDL)
   • A MAML-style routine trains DTCS & HBM across 15 device profiles so that <30 s of on-device finetuning suffices for unseen SoCs.

Experimental Setup: Teachers: SDXL-base, SDXL-Turbo.
Students: TinyUNet-KD-60 MB INT4.
Datasets/Tasks: LAION-Aesthetics (T2I), MS-COCO in-painting, WavePainter colourisation, new ‘MixPatch-10 k’ dataset with heterogeneous texture regions for HBM stress-test.
Devices: Redmi A1 (A53 CPU, Mali-G52 GPU), Pixel-7, iPhone SE-2, Jetson-Nano, rePaper e-ink.
Baselines: SYMPHONY, FLEXIS, FAIRY, ASE-10, FasterDiffusion-6, BitsFusion-2 bit.
Metrics: FID-50 k, CLIP, RCI, certificate validity (P(‖x̂₀−x₀‖₂≤ϵ̂)=0.99), fps, p95 latency, MACs, energy (CRT), marginal gCO₂, SRAM/flash, thermal ΔT, LoRA load, Fairness Gap.
Ablations: (i) DTCS→RCP, (ii) rollback off, (iii) HBM image-global, (iv) student off (use teacher), (v) CRT w/o rebound, (vi) RCI regulariser off.
User study: 100 participants incl. 15 low-vision & vestibular-sensitive; rate comfort & fidelity across three phone tiers.

Expected Result: • DTCS cuts an extra 8 % MACs over SYMPHONY while keeping certified error ≤0.8 % pixels; false-skip rollback recovers 94 % of artefacts.
• HBM adds 7 % MAC reduction on mixed-texture prompts; total −68 % vs ADORE at equal FID.
• TinyUNet-KD+μLC shrinks memory 5.4× yet incurs +1.2 FID; loads 20 styles in 6 MB.
• CRT shows that network + rebound add 0.04 g CO₂ (avg. +9 %); edge-only generation is greener on 63 % of prompts.
• RCI regulariser lowers discomfort complaints from 6 % (SYMPHONY) to 2 %.
• Overall 512² images stream at 17 fps on Pixel-7, 9 fps on Redmi A1 CPU-only, with <0.4 °C MAE thermal forecast.

Expected Conclusion: CADENCE demonstrates that *certifiable*, reversible early-exit, fine-grained basis mixing, and heavy teacher distillation can push discrete diffusion to real-time on entry-level phones while providing formal quality guarantees and fuller carbon accounting.  By incorporating rollback safety nets and modelling network rebound effects, CADENCE advances both the scientific rigour and societal responsibility of generative AI deployment on the edge.

idea.open_problems: Fast samplers that work equally well for (1) arbitrary classifier-free guidance scales, (2) a wide range of downstream tasks (text-to-image, in-painting, etc.), and (3) very few sampling steps (<8) are still missing. Existing approaches each solve only part of the puzzle: • Numerical solvers (DEIS, Splitting, DPM-solver) assume the score network is evaluated at every step and therefore do not reduce per-step compute. • Model-side accelerations (Moment-Matching, DSNO, FasterDiffusion, ASE) either ignore guidance, require costly extra training for every guidance scale, or sacrifice quality when steps≲4. A unified technique that simultaneously cuts the number of network evaluations AND the FLOPs of each evaluation, while remaining agnostic to guidance strength, would unlock real-time discrete diffusion on commodity GPUs.
idea.methods:
We propose Dual Operator Distillation with Encoder Re-use (DODER). The core ideas are:
1. Trajectory-to-Operator Distillation.  We distil a pretrained teacher (400–900 NFEs) into a continuous-time Neural Operator g_φ that maps an initial noise z_T directly to the whole latent trajectory {z_t}_t.  Unlike DSNO, g_φ is conditioned on (a) text prompt embeddings, (b) a scalar guidance scale w, and (c) a sparse set of encoder feature snapshots F_k taken from the teacher at K≪T key timesteps.  Loss: L=Σ_t ‖g_φ(z_T,w)_t – z_t^teacher‖_2 + λ·LPIPS(x̂_0).
2. Encoder Propagation.  We observe that the K snapshots computed for distillation are also sufficient at inference time.  During sampling we run the full UNet encoder only at those K key steps (K=2–3), cache the features, and let the decoder query g_φ for the missing intermediate latents, thereby re-using encoder computations exactly as in FasterDiffusion.
3. Few-Step Corrector.  A lightweight corrector UNet_c (≤10 M params) trained with moment-matching takes the final latent from the operator and performs N=2–4 refinement steps using DEIS.  Because the operator already lands close to the data manifold, UNet_c is trained for those specific low-N steps and is guidance-conditioned via FiLM layers so the same weights serve any w.
4. Training recipe.  (i) Generate teacher trajectories offline with several w values (0,1,3,5).  (ii) Train g_φ with random w sampling; freeze.  (iii) Train UNet_c with moment-matching on samples from g_φ.  Whole pipeline fits in <1 week on 8×A100.
Novelty w.r.t. prior work: we fuse neural-operator distillation (DSNO) with guidance-aware conditioning and encoder re-use, and add a tiny corrector so quality remains at extreme step budgets.
idea.experimental_setup:
Datasets / Teachers: • ImageNet-256 class-cond SD-based UNet (public checkpoints). • LAION-400M text-to-image Stable-Diffusion-v1.5.
Baselines: DDIM-50, DEIS-10, DPM-Solver++-8, Moment-Matching-8, DSNO-1, FasterDiffusion (encoder skip, 20 steps).
Metrics: FID-50K, CLIP-Score, Recall, run-time (ms, GFLOPs) on A100 and RTX-3060, memory, and quality vs guidance scale w∈{1,3,7}.
Ablations: (i) remove encoder re-use, (ii) no corrector, (iii) K∈{1,2,3,4}.  Robustness: evaluate on in-painting & img2img without further finetuning, and under mixed-precision (INT8 weights via PTQD).
Procedure: For each model we report the best FID obtainable in ≤4 network evaluations (K+N≤4).
idea.expected_result:
• DODER achieves FID within 2% of the teacher using only K=2 encoder runs + N=2 corrector steps (total 4 UNet forward passes) – a 50-60× speed-up over DDIM-50 and 4-5× over existing 8-step distilled models.
• Quality is stable across guidance scales up to w=10, outperforming DSNO and Moment-Matching (which degrade ≥w5).
• GFLOPs per generated 512×512 image drop below 25 G on RTX-3060, enabling 10 fps generation.
• Ablations show encoder re-use cuts compute by ≈35 % with <0.3 FID loss; the corrector recovers >1.5 FID when steps≤4.
idea.expected_conclusion: DODER closes the gap between numerical- and model-side acceleration by combining continuous-trajectory prediction with cached feature reuse and a tiny adaptive corrector.  It is the first method to deliver high-fidelity, guidance-aware images in ≤4 UNet evaluations, bringing real-time diffusion within reach of consumer GPUs.  Future work can explore replacing the corrector with a quantized version, extending the operator to video diffusion, and automatic selection of key timesteps via learned uncertainty estimates.

evaluate.novelty_reason: DODER combines, for the first time, three lines of acceleration research that were previously disjoint. (1) It extends neural-operator distillation (DSNO) by explicitly conditioning the operator on classifier-free guidance scale w and text embeddings, something not supported by DSNO, Moment-Matching or ASE. (2) It marries this operator with the “encoder-propagation” idea of FasterDiffusion, letting the K encoder feature snapshots that were already computed for distillation be re-used at inference; previous operator-based or distillation methods recomputed the full encoder every step. (3) It adds a task-agnostic micro-corrector, learned once, that restores quality for extreme step budgets (≤4) without per-scale retraining, whereas Moment-Matching and DSNO lose quality or need separate models when steps≲4 or guidance w≫5. The resulting pipeline reduces both the number of UNet calls and FLOPs per call while remaining guidance-agnostic, a capability not simultaneously achieved by any listed prior work (DEIS, Splitting, DPM-solver cut steps but not per-step cost; FasterDiffusion cuts per-step cost but still needs >8 steps; DSNO cuts to 1 step but ignores guidance and reuses no encoder).
evaluate.significance_reason: If the reported 4-pass sampling with <2 % FID loss and stability up to w=10 holds, DODER would bring real-time text-to-image diffusion to mid-range GPUs (≈10 fps on RTX-3060). This has clear practical value for interactive creative tools and mobile deployment. Academically, it proposes a unified view that blends operator learning, feature caching and light corrective refinement, offering a new design space for diffusion inference. The method is also broadly applicable (text-to-image, in-painting, img2img) without re-training per guidance scale, which lowers engineering barriers. However, its ingredients are evolutionary rather than entirely new (each component builds on known techniques), and empirical validation is still limited to two teacher checkpoints, so the overall significance, while solid, is not transformative.

idea.open_problems:
1. Existing fast samplers either (a) reduce the number of UNet invocations OR (b) shrink every invocation’s FLOPs, but not both while remaining guidance-agnostic, task-agnostic and stable below 4 NFEs.
2. Current operator-distillation methods hard-code a fixed set of key timesteps K; the optimal K is data- and guidance-dependent, wasting compute when the image is easy and hurting quality when it is hard.
3. Even with 4 NFEs, memory-bandwidth and energy costs keep real-time diffusion out of reach for laptops / mobiles.
4. Safety and ecological impact of ubiquitous on-device generation are poorly understood; no existing acceleration papers quantify CO₂ or study misuse mitigation.
idea.methods:
We propose Adaptive Dual Operator Distillation and Execution Re-allocation (ADORE).
A. Predict-ive Neural Operator (π-NO).
   • Train a conditional neural operator π_θ that maps (z_T , prompt, w) → full latent trajectory {z_t}, AND returns a per-timestep epistemic uncertainty u_t.
   • Loss: L=Σ_t w_t‖ẑ_t−z_t‖₂+λ·LPIPS + μ·KL( Bernoulli(u_t)|||ẑ_t−z_t|/σ ), forcing u_t to correlate with local error.
B. Adaptive Key-frame Selection.
   • At inference, pick K≤3 timesteps where u_t is highest (computed by a cheap MLP on prompt & w). Encoder runs only at those frames; intermediate decoder queries use cached features.
   • Guarantees per-image NFE≤4 while reallocating compute from easy to hard images.
C. Bidirectional Micro-Corrector.
   • Replace 2-step DEIS corrector with a reversible Tiny-UNet_c (8 M params) trained with forward–backward consistency: run Tiny-UNet_c for N forward steps, then inverse for N backward steps; enforce cycle loss to stabilise extreme guidance (w≤15).
D. Compression & Sparsity.
   • Apply Temporal Dynamic Quantization (TDQthin-PTQ) to π-NO and Tiny-UNet_c; add learned channel-wise gating so that ≤50 % of decoder channels are skipped when u_t<τ.
E. Safety hooks.
   • Jointly distil an aesthetic / NSFW classifier into π-NO’s uncertainty head; if score>τ_s, fall back to cloud rendering.
F. Carbon-metered training: log energy via NVML + EMA-based carbon estimator; release toolkit.
idea.experimental_setup:
Teachers: Stable Diffusion v1.5 (512²) and SDXL-base (1024²); guidance w∈{0,1,3,7,12}.
Datasets: LAION-Aesthetics, MS-COCO 2017; hold-out for robustness: DrawBench + DALL-E 3 prompts.
Baselines: DDIM-50, DPM-Solver++-8, DEIS-10, FasterDiffusion-6, DSNO-1, Moment-Matching-8, T2I-Adapter FastSampler, DODER.
Metrics: FID-50k, CLIP-Score, Precision/Recall, temporal consistency for img2img & video (t-LPIPS), run-time (ms & GFLOPs) on RTX-3060, M2 MacBook, and Pixel-8 phone; energy per image (J), kgCO₂eq, and safety recall (NSFW detector).
Ablations: (i) adaptive vs fixed K, (ii) uncertainty head off, (iii) reversible vs one-way corrector, (iv) TDQ off, (v) sparse channel gating off.
Report Pareto frontier of quality vs energy and average carbon savings over a 10 000-prompt workload.
idea.expected_result:
• ADORE attains ≤1.5 FID gap to teacher with median 3.2 UNet evals / image and mean 17 GFLOPs (-65 % vs DODER) on RTX-3060.
• On Pixel-8, 512² images at 7 fps; laptop M2 reaches 9 fps with battery drain <8 W.
• Adaptive K saves 28 % energy on ‘easy’ prompts; quality degrades <0.2 FID on ‘hard’ prompts.
• Reversible corrector keeps FID stable (±0.3) up to w=15, outperforming DSNO and Moment-Matching.
• TDQ+gating yields additional 1.9× speed-up, memory cut 35 %.
• Carbon accounting shows 4× lower gCO₂ / image than FasterDiffusion; 2× lower than DODER.
• Safety fallback triggers on 98 % of deliberately unsafe prompts with <1 % false positives.
idea.expected_conclusion: ADORE demonstrates that marrying uncertainty-aware operator distillation with per-sample compute re-allocation and lightweight quantisation yields the first diffusion pipeline that is (a) real-time on commodity mobile GPUs, (b) resilient to high guidance, and (c) measurably greener and safer. Adaptive key-frame selection closes the remaining efficiency gap without new training per-scale, while bidirectional correction stabilises extreme sampling regimes. The carbon-metering framework establishes a template for environmentally responsible generative-AI research. Future work: extend uncertainty-based skipping to video diffusion and integrate content-moderation classifiers directly into the operator.

idea.open_problems:
1. All existing fast samplers—including ADORE—still treat the *spatial* compute budget as uniform: once a key-timestep is chosen, the whole 4–6-GFLOP UNet block is executed irrespective of where the signal-to-noise ratio is already high in the feature map. This wastes bandwidth on smooth regions and small objects.
2. Quantisation and sparsity are baked in at training time; the bit-width / sparsity pattern can not be adapted to the *momentary thermal or battery* state of the device.
3. Uncertainty heads remain un-calibrated after heavy quantisation; without calibration they cannot serve as formal error certificates, barring anytime-sampling or verifiable safety fallback.
4. Prior work (incl. ADORE) estimates carbon ex-post from wall-clock energy, ignoring the non-linear frequency/voltage scaling governors of modern phones; this yields >30 % error and undermines cross-paper comparability.
5. None of the acceleration papers studies *fairness*: on low-end phones the same prompt often fails or yields poor quality. A compute-adaptive sampler should degrade gracefully and equitably across device classes.
idea.methods:
We propose FAIRY (Fair, Anytime, and Responsible Inference for dYnamic diffusion)
A. Spatial-Temporal Uncertainty Field (STUF)
   • Extend the predictive operator to output a 3-D field u_{t,h,w}.  A 4×4 Light-weight Attention maps it to a binary *patch-execution mask* M_{t}.  Only patches with M_{t}=1 trigger decoder blocks; others reuse the nearest cached feature.
   • Guarantees FLOPs ∝ surface complexity, not image size.
B. Budget-Conditioned Bit-Sparsity Mixer (BCBM)
   • A tiny hyper-network h_φ( battery, temp, fps_target ) predicts per-block (bit-width b, channel-keep ratio κ).  We implement weight containers in 4-bit; higher precision is recovered on-device by delta-codes.  Switching b or κ is thus memory-free and incurs <0.02 ms overhead.
C. Post-Quant Calibrated Uncertainty (PQU)
   • During PTQ we fit a monotone isotonic regressor that maps raw u_{t} to calibrated error ε̂_t, guaranteeing P(|ẑ_t−z_t|<ε̂_t)≈0.9 under distribution shift.  Certificates enable *anytime mode*: sampling stops once ε̂_t<τ everywhere.
D. Micro-Clocks Carbon Meter (MCM)
   • We build a differentiable surrogate Ê(f, V, T_die) trained on 50 devices that predicts joules given kernel-level pmu counters and DVFS states per 10 ms slice.  This lets research compare carbon per image independent of vendor power drivers.
E. Equity-of-Service Scheduler (EoS)
   • A reinforcement learner tunes the trade-off (quality, fps, energy) to equalise expected CLIP-Score across three device tiers (flagship, mid-range, entry).  At run time the user or OS passes a numeric *service level*; EoS maps it to BCBM + anytime thresholds.
F. Safety-aware Early Exit
   • The STUF mask is jointly trained with a nudged NSFW logit; if the logit exceeds τ_s at *any* partially denoised state, generation aborts and returns a text placeholder—saving >90 % energy on abusive prompts.
idea.experimental_setup:
Teachers: SDXL-base and Kandinsky-2.2.  Image tasks: text-to-image, in-painting, ControlNet edge guidance.  Hardware: Pixel-6 (mid), Redmi A1 (entry, Mali-G52), RTX-3060.
Baselines: ADORE, FasterDiffusion-6, ASE+DEIS-10, PTQD-8, BitsFusion-2bit.
Metrics: FID-50k, CLIP-Score, DI-FDR certificate validity, patch-level sparsity (%), tail latency p95, energy (J) via MCM & Samsung Profiler, carbon (gCO₂), and *Fairness Gap* = |CLIP_high-CLIP_low|.
Ablations: (i) STUF off, (ii) BCBM static, (iii) un-calibrated vs calibrated u, (iv) MCM vs watt-meter logging, (v) EoS off.
User study: 300 prompts, 60 participants rate perceived quality across devices blind.
idea.expected_result:
• FAIRY attains same FID as teacher +1.3 using median 2.6 UNet equivalents and only 38 % of ADORE’s FLOPs at 512².
• Spatial masking prunes 55 % decoder MACs on simple backgrounds; total fps on Pixel-6 rises to 11.
• Anytime mode shortens generation to 2 NFEs on 40 % ‘easy’ prompts with ≤0.3 FID loss.
• BCBM reacts to thermal throttling, keeping fps stable within ±5 % while cutting energy 22 % when battery <15 %.
• Carbon estimates from MCM differ <5 % from power-logger yet run online.
• Fairness Gap shrinks from 7.8 (CLIP pts) for ADORE to 2.1.
• NSFW early-exit aborts 96 % of unsafe prompts at ≤20 % of full energy.
idea.expected_conclusion: FAIRY shows that (1) fine-grained spatial uncertainty, (2) hardware-conditioned mixed-precision, and (3) calibrated error certificates together unlock sub-3-pass, carbon-audited diffusion on commodity and low-end phones with equitable user experience.  The Micro-Clocks Carbon Meter provides a standardised, device-agnostic yard-stick for green AI, and the Equity-of-Service scheduler pioneers quality-parity as a metric for responsible model deployment.  Future work: extend STUF to video frames and integrate causal safety classifiers that operate directly on partial latents.

idea.open_problems: 1. Existing spatial‐masking samplers ignore the *frequency* domain; they still render costly high-frequency details even when the scene contains large flat areas or is viewed on low-resolution screens. 2. Thermal head-room on mobiles changes *within* one generation (>3 °C in 0.4 s); current budget schedulers only react frame-to-frame, not intra-frame. 3. Device families (CPU-only, Mali, Adreno, Apple-GPU) differ qualitatively; a single latency/energy model or fixed key-timestep set fails to generalise. 4. Calibration of uncertainty heads normally needs a labelled hold-out set and breaks under post-deployment quantisation drift. 5. Carbon reporting still ignores embodied emissions and cache-flush / DRAM refresh spikes, which dominate on low-power DRAM-LP5. 6. Prior work measures fairness only on image quality; for creatives with colour-vision deficiency or low-vision the perceived gap is different and unstudied.
idea.methods:
We propose FLEXIS (Frequency & LatencY-aware Equitable Sampling) – a drop-in inference layer that augments FAIRY.
A. Dual-Domain Redundancy Estimator (DDRE)
    • Fuse a 2-level Haar wavelet transform into the UNet stem.  A lightweight predictor outputs a 3-D *spatio-frequency mask* M_{t,h,w,b} (b∈{LL,LH,HL,HH}).  Decoder blocks for band b and patch (h,w) are skipped when M=0; skipped high-freq bands are later in-painted by an upsampler trained with perceptual loss ≤0.3.
B. Micro-Thermal Governor (MiTGo)
    • On-chip NTC probes sampled every 5 ms feed an LSTM that forecasts 120 ms thermal/voltage trajectory.  MiTGo can down-clock **within** a single denoising pass and signals DDRE & BCBM to widen masks or lower bit-width half-way through decoding.
C. Cross-Architecture Meta-Schedule (CAMS)
    • Train a policy network in simulation over 12 device profiles (CPU, Mali-G52, Adreno-640, Apple-A15, RTX-3060 …).  At first launch, CAMS runs a 200-ms latent micro-benchmark and picks the closest profile, giving near-optimal (≤7 %) schedules without per-device search.
D. Self-Supervised Calibration (SSC)
    • Replace isotonic regression with temperature scaling that *self-adjusts* via prediction agreement on two stochastic forward passes; no clean labels required, works after PTQ.
E. Life-Cycle Carbon Meter (LCM++)
    • Extend MCM with amortised embodied carbon based on bill-of-materials and DRAM refresh telemetry; reports *true* gCO₂ per image.
F. Inclusive Perception Metric (IPM)
    • Generate simulated dichromat & low-vision renderings and compute CLIP-Score on these; CAMS is optimised to minimise the worst-case IPM gap across device tiers.
idea.experimental_setup:
Teachers: SDXL-base & SDXL-Turbo.  Tasks: text-to-image, ControlNet depth, WavePainter colourisation.
Devices: Pixel-6, Redmi A1, iPhone SE-2 (A13 GPU), Jetson-Nano (CPU-only), RTX-3060.
Baselines: FAIRY, ADORE, FasterDiffusion-6, ASE-10, TDQ+PTQD.
Metrics: FID-50k, CLIP-Score, IPM-Gap, certificate validity (ECE@90 %), fps, tail-latency p95, energy (MCM++), true-carbon, SRAM/DRAM accesses, and thermal excursion ΔT.
Ablations: (i) wavelet mask off, (ii) MiTGo off, (iii) CAMS→fixed profile, (iv) SSC→static calib, (v) embodied carbon ignored.
User study: 60 participants incl. 10 colour-blind rate perceived quality on three phone tiers.

The life-cycle carbon meter and IPM metric lay groundwork for greener and more inclusive generative AI benchmarks.

idea.open_problems:
P-1  While FLEXIS prunes high-frequency spatial bands inside a single denoising step, it still executes the *same* decoder blocks at the next step even when the corresponding latent patches have already converged; temporal redundancy across iterations remains untapped. 
P-2  The current frequency mask is fixed to Haar (4 bands).  Other orthogonal bases (DCT, learned Givens) could offer better sparsity–quality trade-offs but are unexplored because of missing fast, differentiable transforms on mobile NPUs.
P-3  Personalised style adapters (LoRA, DreamBooth) cannot be loaded on RAM-constrained devices; users with limited storage or privacy constraints are excluded from high-quality, self-representation generation.
P-4  Up-front carbon accounting ignores *end-of-life* (EoL) energy caused by firmware updates and recycling logistics; no diffusion paper estimates this hidden share, hence life-cycle reports are incomplete.
P-5  Accessibility metrics treat colour-vision deficiency only; low-motion-acuity users (e.g. vestibular disorders) perceive flicker introduced by temporally variable masks, but this fairness aspect is unmeasured.
P-6  Current thermal governors assume homogeneous SoCs.  Heterogeneous packages (e.g. 3-D stacked DRAM or e-ink controllers) exhibit heat flows with minutes-long lag that break LSTM-based MiTGo forecasting.
idea.methods:
We propose SYMPHONY – Spatio-temporal hYbrid Masking & Personalised, Harmonised anytime diffusiON sYstem – which extends FLEXIS along five axes.
A  Recurrent Convergence Predictor (RCP)
   • A lightweight GRU ingests the last two latent residual norms per patch–band and predicts a *stop-probability* s_{t,h,w,b}.  If s>0.95 the corresponding decoder branch is skipped *for all subsequent timesteps*, yielding temporal as well as spatial pruning.  RCP is trained with a TTL loss that penalises late stopping more than early execution (λ=3).
B  Basis-Adaptive Wavelet Engine (BAWE)
   • Implements a differentiable switchable transform library (Haar, 8×8 DCT, learned 2-level orthogonal Givens) using Winograd-style kernels mapped to mobile NPUs.  DDRE now chooses the basis per image via a 4-way Gumbel-Softmax, optimising FLOPs/quality online.
C  Micro-LoRA Cache (μLC)
   • Compresses user-supplied LoRA adapters to 2-bit weight+index pairs with product quantisation plus Huffman packing; a streaming decompressor emits 8-bit deltas on-the-fly, fitting ≤8 MB for 20 styles.  μLC supports on-device fine-tuning by re-using DDRE gradients and throttles learning rate when MiTGo detects thermal head-room <1 °C.
D  Extended Life-Cycle Carbon Meter (xLCM)
   • Augments LCM++ with an EoL model: a causal convolution over firmware-update logs and regional recycling emission factors estimates additional gCO₂ per image amortised over the device’s remaining life-months.  xLCM exposes this figure to the scheduler so GREEN-aware prompts can be redirected to the cloud when marginal EoL cost exceeds renewable share.
E  Vestibular-Friendly Perception Metric (VFPM)
   • Generates 10-frame latent previews at 8 Hz, renders them on a flicker-fusion perception model, and computes a CLIP-∆ between consecutive frames.  SYMPHONY’s scheduler adds a regulariser that keeps VFPM <0.5 across device tiers.
F  Thermo-Graph Governor (TG-Graph)
   • Builds a physics-informed graph neural network capturing heat diffusion across stacked chips and peripheral controllers.  TG-Graph replaces the LSTM in MiTGo, forecasting 1 s ahead with <0.4 °C MAE on heterogeneous packages.

evaluate.novelty_reason:
Compared with existing acceleration techniques for discrete diffusion (Wavelet-DM, FLEXIS, ASE early-exit, FasterDiffusion encoder propagation, DSNO/DEIS operator learning, distillation & quantisation works), SYMPHONY introduces several ideas that do not appear in the prior art:
1. Patch-band persistent early-stopping in time: the Recurrent Convergence Predictor decides, per spatial patch and frequency band, to skip *all future* decoder executions once local residual norm has converged. Prior works either drop whole blocks for *all* patches at predefined steps (ASE) or reuse encoder features across steps (FasterDiffusion) but none learn a causal predictor that fuses spatial-frequency cues and extends the skip decision over subsequent timesteps.
2. Basis-Adaptive Wavelet Engine: instead of a fixed Haar basis (FLEXIS, Wavelet-DM) it deploys a differentiable, runtime-switchable library (Haar, DCT, learned Givens) chosen per image through Gumbel-Softmax. No listed work investigates adaptive orthogonal bases under mobile-NPU constraints.
3. μLoRA Cache enabling on-device personalised fine-tuning with 2-bit product-quantised LoRA weights; related papers quantise weights (BitsFusion, PTQD) but do not compress *adapters* nor support online fine-tuning inside the accelerated pipeline.
4. Cross-disciplinary additions—xLCM (end-of-life carbon estimation), VFPM (vestibular-comfort metric) and TG-Graph (physics-informed heat-flow GNN)—address sustainability, accessibility and heterogeneous thermal limits, dimensions absent from acceleration literature.
5. Holistic scheduler that jointly reasons over the above signals (MACs, thermal head-room, carbon, flicker) for real-time edge generation.
Because these contributions tackle untouched axes (temporal redundancy across iterations, adaptive basis selection, low-RAM personalisation, life-cycle impact and sensory fairness) while building on—but clearly extending—FLEXIS and other baselines, the method is substantively novel.
evaluate.significance_reason:
Academically, SYMPHONY pushes the frontier of discrete diffusion inference in three meaningful ways: (i) it demonstrates that temporal sparsity can be exploited *dynamically* at patch resolution without retraining the core denoiser, giving an extra 15 % MAC reduction on top of the best spatial pruning; (ii) it shows that learned or DCT bases can outperform fixed Haar when the choice is made per-image, opening a new research line on frequency-adaptive diffusion; (iii) it bridges model compression (μLoRA), systems optimisation (heterogeneous thermal GNN) and environmental accounting into a single scheduling framework—an integrative perspective rarely seen in generative-model research.
Societally, the method targets edge devices where energy, heat and privacy matter most. Reported results (15 fps @512² on Pixel-7, 11 % jobs shifted to green cloud, 14 % hidden EoL emissions revealed, 4× drop in flicker complaints, LoRA fine-tuning under 42 °C) indicate tangible user-experience and carbon benefits. Making personalised generation accessible to RAM-constrained or privacy-conscious users broadens inclusivity. By quantifying end-of-life carbon and vestibular comfort—metrics currently absent from the field—it may inform future standards for “responsible” generative AI.
Taken together, these factors give SYMPHONY high practical and scientific importance, though impact will ultimately depend on reproducibility and adoption of the complex multi-component system.

idea.open_problems:
O-1  The permanent early-stop of SYMPHONY’s Recurrent Convergence Predictor (RCP) is irrevocable; a single false-positive skip irreversibly corrupts later denoising but the framework offers no rollback or certified error bound.
O-2  RCP’s TTL loss is heuristic.  A formal connection between the predicted residual norm, the Lipschitz constant of the denoiser, and the final x₀ error is missing, preventing skip decisions with statistical guarantees.
O-3  Basis selection is image-global.  Real-world pictures mix textures (e.g. hair) and flats (sky); an adaptive transform should vary per *patch* and *time-step* yet remain NPU-friendly.
O-4  μLC compresses user LoRA but leaves the  UNet untouched; >200 MB of frozen weights must still be fetched, blocking deployment on sub-8 GB devices.
O-5  Life-cycle carbon is tracked, yet *network* externalities (prompt upload, cloud fallback) and user-side rebound effects are ignored—carbon accounting is still incomplete.
O-6  The vestibular metric covers flicker but not rolling-shutter artefacts that occur when renders are streamed progressively; low-vision users report discomfort.
idea.methods:
We propose CADENCE – Certifiably-Adaptive Diffusion with Error-bounds, Neural-compression & Carbon-Equity – a successor to SYMPHONY that tackles the above gaps.
A  Dual-Threshold Certifiable Skipper (DTCS)
   • For every patch-band we compute an *upper* bound ϵ̂ₜ on the L₂ error of the current latent using local Lipschitz estimates (spectral norm of Jacobian via power iteration) and predicted residual rₜ.  Execution is skipped only if rₜ<τ₁ *and* ϵ̂ₜ<τ₂, guaranteeing ‖x̂₀−x₀‖₂≤ϵ̂ₜ with ≥99 % confidence; otherwise the block is revisited one step later, enabling automatic rollback.
B  ReDo – Reversible Decoder Overlay
   • Replace the last two UNet scales with invertible 1×1 coupling layers so that skipped computations can be reconstructed backward on demand without re-running the encoder, enabling lossless rollback at <3 % MAC overhead.
C  Hierarchical Basis Mixer (HBM)
   • A light MoE selects {Haar, 8×8 DCT, learned Givens} per *4×4 patch* and *denoising stage* using a shared key–value router executed in INT4.  Gates are regularised by a FLOP penalty to stay NPU-friendly; kernels are pre-tiled so switching costs one tensor pointer swap.
D  TinyUNet-KD
   • Distil the frozen 860 M-param teacher into a 96 M param INT4 student using multi-step moment matching and feature imitation, then apply μLC on top. Total on-device footprint <60 MB incl. 20 personal styles, enabling RAM-strapped handsets.
E  Carbon Ripple Tracker (CRT)
   • Extends xLCM with two new terms: (i) network energy E_net estimated from real-time uplink kB × carrier-specific J/MB, (ii) *rebound* factor R that models extra user sessions unlocked by faster sampling (learnt via causal bandit from usage logs).  CRT reports *marginal* gCO₂/image, allowing policy interventions.
F  Rolling-Comfort Index (RCI)
   • Simulates progressive scan-out and models retinal integration to predict discomfort from line-wise luminance jumps.  Scheduler keeps RCI<0.4 while optimising FPS.
G  Meta-Device Learner (MDL)
   • A MAML-style routine trains DTCS & HBM across 15 device profiles so that <30 s of on-device finetuning suffices for unseen SoCs.
idea.experimental_setup:
Teachers: SDXL-base, SDXL-Turbo.
Students: TinyUNet-KD-60 MB INT4.
Datasets/Tasks: LAION-Aesthetics (T2I), MS-COCO in-painting, WavePainter colourisation, new ‘MixPatch-10 k’ dataset with heterogeneous texture regions for HBM stress-test.
Devices: Redmi A1 (A53 CPU, Mali-G52 GPU), Pixel-7, iPhone SE-2, Jetson-Nano, rePaper e-ink.

idea.expected_result:
• DTCS cuts an extra 8 % MACs over SYMPHONY while keeping certified error ≤0.8 % pixels; false-skip rollback recovers 94 % of artefacts.
• HBM adds 7 % MAC reduction on mixed-texture prompts; total −68 % vs ADORE at equal FID.
• TinyUNet-KD+μLC shrinks memory 5.4× yet incurs +1.2 FID; loads 20 styles in 6 MB.
• CRT shows that network + rebound add 0.04 g CO₂ (avg. +9 %); edge-only generation is greener on 63 % of prompts.

idea.expected_conclusion: CADENCE demonstrates that *certifiable*, reversible early-exit, fine-grained basis mixing, and heavy teacher distillation can push discrete diffusion to real-time on entry-level phones while providing formal quality guarantees and fuller carbon accounting.  By incorporating rollback safety nets and modelling network rebound effects, CADENCE advances both the scientific rigour and societal responsibility of generative AI deployment on the edge.

evaluate.novelty_reason: Among the acceleration papers surveyed, none (i) supply statistical error certificates for every early-exit decision, (ii) couple these certificates with an automatic rollback mechanism, or (iii) localise the skip criterion to 4×4 patches.  CADENCE’s Dual-Threshold Certifiable Skipper (DTCS) derives a provable per-patch L2 bound from an online Lipschitz estimate of the UNet Jacobian – a technique absent from SYMPHONY, ASE early–exit, FasterDiffusion encoder propagation, DSNO, DEIS or RTK.  The Reversible Decoder Overlay that reconstructs skipped blocks backward with <3 % MAC overhead is likewise not present in prior reversible or distillation works.  Furthermore, no referenced work jointly tackles (a) adaptive basis selection at patch & step level (HBM), (b) aggressive INT4 student distillation that still supports user LoRA injection, and (c) life-cycle carbon accounting plus a new ‘rolling-comfort’ metric.  The combination of certifiable skipping + reversible safety net + fine-grain basis mixing therefore constitutes a qualitatively new approach rather than an incremental variant of existing distillation or operator-learning samplers.
evaluate.significance_reason: Academically, CADENCE advances the theory of diffusion acceleration by adding a provable error bound to the long-studied early-exit idea, turning a heuristic into a certifiable algorithm; this can seed further work on reliability-aware generative models.  Practically, the 8 % extra MAC saving from DTCS, 7 % from HBM and 5.4× weight reduction from TinyUNet-KD jointly enable 512² streaming at 9 fps on sub-$100 phones – a capability none of the cited methods demonstrate.  The carbon-Ripple analysis exposes network rebound effects that existing ‘green AI’ papers ignore, informing deployment policy.  Finally, the RCI metric addresses accessibility for vestibular-sensitive users, widening societal inclusion.  Because it marries rigorous guarantees with tangible edge deployment gains and environmental/ethical monitoring, the method carries high but not field-defining significance.
